newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire lauds U.S. call for closure of Rwanda camps.
newsitem.headline: Zaire lauds U.S. call for closure of Rwanda camps.

text.p: Zaire welcomed a U.S. call for the closure of camps for Rwandan refugees in volatile east Zaire, saying it was now up to international agencies to help avert forced repatriation.
Deputy foreign minister Lokondo Yoka said U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher's call was an important endorsement of Zaire's bid to repatriate the more than a million Hutu refugees.
"But that is not enough," Lokondo told Reuters, adding: "Psychological, social, economic and political pressure must be brought on Kigali to make it accept its Hutu nationals."

"The United States is one of the donors whose agencies operate in the east," Lokondo said. "Most of these agencies oppose the return of refugees to Rwanda. The stand taken by Warren Christopher is a positive development in resolving the problem in eastern Zaire."
Lokondo could not say if forced repatriations halted after a brief start in August would resume, saying that was a decision was for Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo and his full cabinet.
The Tutsi-dominated Rwandan government says Hutus, who fled civil war in 1994 and are blamed for the genocide of up to a million minority Tutsis or Hutu moderates, are free to return.
Hutus fearing reprisals are reluctant to go home.
Zaire blames refugees for insecurity in its eastern region while Rwanda accuses Zaire of doing nothing to stop armed Hutus using refugee camps to stage attacks inside Rwanda.

Zaire forcibly expelled about 15,000 Hutus last August but an international outcry forced it to suspend the action. An accord it reached with the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR for voluntary repatriation has made little progress while parliament maintains pressure on the government to throw out Hutus.
Christopher told a news conference in Tanzania during his five-nation Africa tour that it was safe for Hutus to go home and that their camps in Tanzania and Zaire should be closed.
"We believe it is time to close the camps closest to the Rwandan border that pose the greatest security threat," he said after talks with African leaders on Burundi and Rwanda.
In a written statement issued later, he asserted that the "refugees should be encouraged to return voluntarily to Rwanda" and the U.S. view is that most refugees "can now do so safely".
Christopher is the most senior U.S. official to address the refugee problem, which is potentially more explosive than the crisis involving ethnic Tutsis ordered to leave eastern Zaire.
Only about 200,000 ethnic Tutsis or Banyamulenges are affected by the Tuesday deadline decreed by regional authorities in Zaire's South Kivu Province nearly a week ago.
The central government in Kinshasa, whose hold on regions of the vast country is tenuous, has not declared its stand on the plight of the Tutsis since the deadline was announced.
